title: Honor and shame
seoTitle: Honor and Shame in the Bible's World: What It Was Really Like
description: A long, sourced portrait of the values the Bible's first readers lived by: honor as a public verdict, challenge and envy, kin before self, gift and gratitude, the table and the guest, men and women in public, shame and vindication in Israel's Scriptures, and the cross that turned the scale over.
line: What a good name was worth, how it was won and lost, and what the gospel did to the scale, with the evidence named as we go and the arguments over it stated plainly.
intro: This is a portrait of the values the people of the Bible lived by: honor and shame, the family name, the contest in the open street, the gift and the debt of thanks, the guest at the table, the envious eye, the place of men and women in public, and the cross that turned the whole scale over. The portraits of Jewish life in Jesus's day and of the Roman world on this site already show the house, the patron and the dinner. This one goes underneath them to the values that made those things matter so much to the people who lived them.

Some of the evidence is ancient and plain. Aristotle, Seneca, Plutarch, Philo, Ben Sira and Josephus wrote about honor, gifts and gratitude in their own words, and cities carved their thanks to benefactors in stone. But the frame most readers meet today comes from modern anthropology. Studies of village life around the Mediterranean in the 1950s and 1960s, gathered in J. G. Peristiany's volume Honour and Shame (1965), were applied to the New Testament by Bruce Malina in The New Testament World (1981), and then by Jerome Neyrey, John Elliott and others in the Context Group, a working group of biblical scholars that took shape in the late 1980s. David deSilva made the approach widely readable in Honor, Patronage, Kinship and Purity (2000).

That frame has serious critics, and the page names them where they matter. Among anthropologists, Michael Herzfeld argued in 1980 that the words honor and shame glossed over many different local ideas, and others doubted the Mediterranean was one culture at all. In biblical studies, F. Gerald Downing (1999) showed that honor in one's own community was not always the first concern of ancient writers, Louise Lawrence (2003) judged the models too rigid, and Zeba Crook (2009) kept the model but corrected it. Two more cautions hold for every part. No culture runs only on shame while another runs only on guilt: the contrast goes back to Ruth Benedict's study of Japan (1946) and E. R. Dodds's use of it for early Greece (1951), and both allowed for mixtures. And nothing here describes any living people. Where a modern village custom is mentioned, such as those Kenneth Bailey reported from long years in the Middle East, it is marked as a modern parallel, not ancient evidence.

parts.title: A public verdict
parts.line: Honor was the worth other people granted you, and it belonged to a family as much as to a person.
body: In the world of the Bible, honor was not first a feeling inside a person. It was a judgment made outside, by the people whose opinion counted, about what a person and a family were worth. Bruce Malina's working definition has two halves: the worth a person claims, and the group's acknowledgment of that claim. If the town granted the claim, you had honor. If it refused, you did not, whatever you thought of yourself. Zeba Crook, revising Malina in the Journal of Biblical Literature (2009), put the point more sharply still: the public court of reputation had the power to define honor and shame as it pleased.

Ancient writers said as much in their own words. Aristotle called honor the greatest of the external goods (Nicomachean Ethics 4.3, 1123b). The usual Hebrew word for glory and honor, kavod, comes from a root that means heavy. A person of honor carried weight. When the psalmist asks, "How long, O men, will my honor be maligned?" (Psalm 4:2), that is the word he uses, and the complaint is about his name in other people's mouths.

Some honor came with birth. Anthropologists call it ascribed honor (Crook suggested attributed honor as the better term): the worth of your family, your town and your people, given before you had done anything. The rest was acquired, won through generosity, courage, skill, office and the small contests of daily life. Because birth mattered, a family tree was an honor document. Josephus opens the account of his own life with his pedigree, priestly on his father's side and descended from the Hasmonean kings on his mother's, and says he set it down as he found it in the public records (Life 1 to 6). Paul gives his own list to the Philippians: "circumcised on the eighth day, of the people of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin; a Hebrew of Hebrews; as to the law, a Pharisee" (Philippians 3:5). Then he does what no honor list was meant to do, and calls it loss.

Matthew's Gospel opens the same way: "the record of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham" (Matthew 1:1). Jerome Neyrey, in Honor and Shame in the Gospel of Matthew (1998), read the whole Gospel as an encomium, the ancient speech of praise that began with a person's birth and ancestry and went on to his deeds. Yet this list of the highest honor names four women whose stories a rival could have used against it: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth the Moabite, and the one Matthew calls only "Uriah's wife" (Matthew 1:3, 5 to 6). The genealogy claims the throne of David and does not hide the scandals on the way to it.

Ascribed honor could also close a door. When Jesus taught in the synagogue at Nazareth, the people who heard him asked where he had got such wisdom, and answered their own question with his family: "Isn't this the carpenter, the son of Mary and the brother of James, Joses, Judas, and Simon?" (Mark 6:3). They knew his house, so they knew his worth, and his words did not fit it. Mark says they took offense. In a world where worth was granted by those who knew you best, the people who had watched a man grow up were the hardest court to win.

Honor also belonged to groups more than to persons. A son's disgrace fell on his father, a daughter's on her household, a disciple's on his teacher, a citizen's on his city. That is one reason the Gospels and Paul's letters speak so much of being ashamed of someone or not: to stand next to a disgraced person was to share the disgrace. Paul thanks God for Onesiphorus, who "was unashamed of my chains" (2 Timothy 1:16), and Jesus warns that whoever is ashamed of him will find the Son of Man ashamed of them (Mark 8:38).

The model helps, and it has been pressed too far. F. Gerald Downing, in "'Honor' among Exegetes" (Catholic Biblical Quarterly, 1999), argued that ancient writers did not always put honor in their own community first, and asked whether modern Westerners are really so free of the concern. Crook argued that the honor contest was not only a game between equal men; people challenged across lines of rank and between men and women. The fair reading is that honor mattered everywhere in this world without explaining everything in it, and that people argued about what was honorable. Jesus's own question takes two courts for granted: "How can you believe if you accept glory from one another, yet do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?" (John 5:44).

read.text: When the Sabbath came, He began to teach in the synagogue, and many who heard Him were astonished. “Where did this man get these ideas?” they asked. “What is this wisdom He has been given? And how can He perform such miracles? Isn’t this the carpenter, the son of Mary and the brother of James, Joses, Judas, and Simon? Aren’t His sisters here with us as well?” And they took offense at Him. Then Jesus said to them, “Only in his hometown, among his relatives, and in his own household is a prophet without honor.”
read.note: The townspeople don't dispute the wisdom or the miracles, only where they could have come from, given the family they know. Mark names the brothers and sisters so the reader can feel the weight of the village's verdict, and Jesus's proverb names the court that refused him: his hometown, his relatives, his own household.

read.text: But whatever was gain to me I count as loss for the sake of Christ. More than that, I count all things as loss compared to the surpassing excellence of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord, for whom I have lost all things. I consider them rubbish, that I may gain Christ
read.note: These verses follow a list of inherited and earned honor: the right circumcision, the right tribe, the strictest party, the zeal to prove it. Paul doesn't say the list was false. He says he's moved it from the gain column to the loss column, and his word for it is rubbish. To readers in a Roman colony proud of its rank, that was a startling way to talk about a good name.

read.text: How can you believe if you accept glory from one another, yet do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?
read.note: Jesus names the problem in the language of honor. The word translated glory is the same word used for a person's standing. Those who live for the approval of one another's court, he says, cannot easily hear the verdict of God's. The verse takes the whole honor system seriously and refuses to let it be the final judge.

parts.title: Challenge, reply and the evil eye
parts.line: Honor was won and lost in public exchanges, and a world that thought good things were scarce feared the envious eye.
body: The French sociologist Pierre Bourdieu studied honor among the Kabyle villagers of Algeria, and his essay in Peristiany's 1965 volume described an exchange he called challenge and riposte. A man challenges another in public. The challenge is worth answering only if it comes from an equal. The other must reply, and the onlookers decide who won; to be ignored altogether was worse than losing. Malina and others then read the controversy stories of the Gospels with this pattern in mind. A study of modern Algerian villages is not ancient evidence, so the real test is whether the Gospels show the pattern on their own. Often they do.

Take the question about taxes. Mark says the Pharisees and Herodians were sent "to catch Jesus in His words" (Mark 12:13). They open with praise: "we know that You are honest and seek favor from no one" (12:14). Then they put a question before the crowd with two losing answers. Say yes, and he sides with Rome against his people; say no, and he is a rebel. Jesus asks for a coin, asks whose image is on it, and gives his answer, "and they marveled at Him" (12:17). Luke tells the end of the scene as a public result: "they were unable to trap Him in His words before the people; and amazed at His answer, they fell silent" (Luke 20:26).

The same shape recurs. When the chief priests ask by what authority he acts, Jesus answers with a question about John the Baptist, and when they will not commit themselves he declines to answer them (Mark 11:27 to 33). When a synagogue leader scolds the crowd for coming to be healed on the Sabbath, the reproach is aimed at Jesus through them (Luke 13:14), and Luke records what the room decided: "all His adversaries were humiliated. And the whole crowd rejoiced" (13:17). Matthew closes a long day of such questions with the scoreboard: "from that day on no one dared to question Him any further" (Matthew 22:46).

Crook's correction matters here, because the contest wasn't only between equal men. A Greek woman of Syrophoenician origin asks Jesus to heal her daughter, is answered with a hard saying about bread for the children and not the dogs, and replies: "even the dogs under the table eat the children's crumbs." Jesus grants her request "because of this answer" (Mark 7:28 to 29). Scholars read that exchange in more than one way, but on any reading a foreign woman spoke back in public and was honored for it.

Beneath the contests lay an assumption anthropologists call limited good. An American anthropologist, in an article titled "Peasant Society and the Image of Limited Good" (American Anthropologist, 1965, listed in the sources below), drew on fieldwork in a Mexican village to describe peasants who saw land, wealth, health, friendship and honor as existing in fixed amounts, so that one family could rise only at another's expense. Malina applied the idea to the biblical world. It is a modern model, and it should be used as a lens, not a law. But the Bible has scenes it fits. When the women of Israel sang, "Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands," Saul heard praise given to David as praise taken from himself: "What more can he have but the kingdom?" (1 Samuel 18:7 to 8).

Where good is scarce, envy is dangerous, and the ancient world believed envy could strike through the eye. Plutarch's Table Talk (5.7) records a dinner conversation about people said to cast the evil eye, in which one guest argues that envy, lodged in the mind, sends harm out through the eyes like poisoned darts. A floor mosaic of the second century AD from a house at Antioch, now in the Hatay Archaeology Museum, shows a great eye attacked by a raven, a dog, a scorpion, a snake and other creatures and pierced by a trident, with two Greek words that turn the curse back on the envier: kai su, "you too." John H. Elliott gathered the evidence from Mesopotamia to the early church in four volumes, Beware the Evil Eye (2015 to 2017).

The idiom runs through the Bible. In Mark's list of what comes out of the heart, the word the Berean Standard Bible translates "envy" is in Greek "an evil eye" (Mark 7:22), and the Hebrew behind the "stingy man" of Proverbs 23:6 is a man evil of eye. In the parable of the workers, the landowner's last question is, in Greek, "Is your eye evil because I am good?" which the Berean Standard Bible renders "are you envious because I am generous?" (Matthew 20:15). Paul's "Who has bewitched you?" (Galatians 3:1) uses baskaino, the ordinary verb for casting the evil eye, its only use in the New Testament; how literally he meant it is argued. Pilate himself, in Mark's telling, "knew it was out of envy that the chief priests had handed Jesus over" (Mark 15:10).

read.text: And they were unable to trap Him in His words before the people; and amazed at His answer, they fell silent.
read.note: Luke reports the outcome the way the crowd would have scored it. The trap was meant to be sprung before the people, and it failed before the people. Their silence is the point: in a public contest, the side with nothing left to say had lost.

read.text: Do I not have the right to do as I please with what is mine? Or are you envious because I am generous?’
read.note: The Greek idiom is the evil eye. The workers hired at dawn received exactly what they agreed to, yet the landowner's goodness to the latecomers feels to them like a loss of their own. In a world that thought good things were limited, that was the natural reaction. The parable asks the hearer to see generosity without counting it as theft.

read.text: For he knew it was out of envy that the chief priests had handed Jesus over.
read.note: Mark gives the motive of the chief priests in one word. Envy was counted among the most dangerous of passions, the one that could not bear another's rise. Pilate, an outsider to the contest, could see it. The Gospel lets the reader see that the cross began, among other things, as the work of a jealous eye.

parts.title: Kin before self
parts.line: A person was known by a father, a town and a people, and the church dared to call strangers brothers and sisters.
body: Names in the Gospels carry families and places with them: Simon son of Jonah, James and John the sons of Zebedee, Jesus of Nazareth, Saul of Tarsus. The first thing a stranger needed to know was whose you were. A person was placed by a father, a household, a village and a people before anything was known of his own gifts, and his first loyalties ran back along those lines. The site's guide on singular and plural "you" follows this into Paul's letters, which were written almost entirely to groups.

That's why leaving family appears in the Gospels as a real cost, not a stage of growing up. James and John "left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired men" (Mark 1:20), walking out of the family business in front of the men it employed. Few duties weighed more than burying a father; Joseph has to ask Pharaoh's leave to do it, and does so in those words: "let me go and bury my father, and then return" (Genesis 50:5). So when a would-be disciple asks for the same leave and hears, "Follow Me, and let the dead bury their own dead" (Matthew 8:21 to 22), the saying lands as an offense against the most honored bond a son had.

Jesus did not abolish kinship. He redrew it. When his mother and brothers came to fetch him, he pointed to his disciples: "Here are My mother and My brothers. For whoever does the will of My Father in heaven is My brother and sister and mother" (Matthew 12:49 to 50). He told his followers not to be called Rabbi, because "you are all brothers," and to call no one on earth father, "for you have one Father, who is in heaven" (Matthew 23:8 to 9). He promised that those who left houses and families for his sake would receive a hundredfold, houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children, in this age, along with persecutions (Mark 10:29 to 30). The new family came with a new household, and with trouble.

Anthropologists call this fictive kinship: family language and family duties among people not related by blood. Joseph Hellerman, in When the Church Was a Family (2009), argues that the early church chose the strongest bond its world knew, the bond between brothers and sisters, the one relationship a person could not resign. The letters speak this way without strain. Hebrews says Jesus "is not ashamed to call them brothers" (Hebrews 2:11). Paul calls the church "the family of faith" (Galatians 6:10). A young pastor is told to treat older men as fathers, younger men as brothers, older women as mothers and younger women as sisters (1 Timothy 5:1 to 2).

Outsiders noticed, and not kindly. The satirist Lucian, writing soon after AD 165 about a charlatan who had spent time among the Christians, mocks them because their first lawgiver persuaded them they were all brothers once they had denied the Greek gods and worshiped "that crucified sophist" (The Passing of Peregrinus 13, in A. M. Harmon's translation). About AD 197 Tertullian, defending the Christians of North Africa, reports that pagans were angry that Christians called one another brothers, and that they said, half in scorn, how these people love one another (Apology 39, paraphrased).

The new family could set the old one at odds, and the critics said so. The philosopher Celsus, writing in the later second century and quoted by Origen in his reply, complained that wool workers, cobblers and laundry workers in private houses would get children alone and tell them not to listen to their fathers and teachers but to them (Origen, Against Celsus 3.55). Jesus had said as much would happen: "A man's enemies will be the members of his own household" (Matthew 10:36, quoting Micah 7:6). Yet the New Testament also holds the natural family to its duties. A man who "does not provide for his own, and especially his own household," is "worse than an unbeliever" (1 Timothy 5:8). The church didn't dissolve the household; it set a larger family around it.

read.text: But Jesus replied, “Who is My mother, and who are My brothers?” Pointing to His disciples, He said, “Here are My mother and My brothers. For whoever does the will of My Father in heaven is My brother and sister and mother.”
read.note: His mother and brothers are standing outside, which in a household-centered world was a claim on him. Jesus doesn't deny them. He enlarges the circle and names the rule of entry: doing the will of the Father. In a world where you were born into your family, this family is joined by obedience.

read.text: For both the One who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are of the same family. So Jesus is not ashamed to call them brothers.
read.note: To own someone as kin in public was to share his standing, high or low. Hebrews says the Son is not ashamed to do it. The same letter later says that God "is not ashamed to be called their God" (Hebrews 11:16). The language of honor runs both ways: God claims people the world would be ashamed to claim.

read.text: Do not rebuke an older man, but appeal to him as to a father. Treat younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, and younger women as sisters, with absolute purity.
read.note: These are family duties transferred to a congregation: respect for fathers, care for mothers, the easy speech of brothers, the protected honor of sisters. For many converts, especially slaves and those cut off by their own families, the church was not like a family. It was the only family they had.

parts.title: Gift, gratitude and loyalty
parts.line: A gift bound giver and receiver together, gratitude was a public duty, and faith meant keeping faith.
body: The site's guide on patronage and grace explains how the Greek word charis covered the giver's favor, the gift and the thanks. This part goes to the values underneath. The fullest ancient discussion is Seneca's long treatise On Benefits, written by Paul's contemporary in the middle of the first century. Seneca says that the giving and returning of benefits is the practice that most of all binds human society together (1.4.2). He opens the book with the Three Graces: some, he says, read them as one who gives, one who receives and one who returns, and they dance in a ring because a benefit passes from hand to hand and comes back to the giver (1.3). Gratitude, in this picture, was not a private glow. It was the public return of honor: praise, loyalty and service, seen by all.

That's why ingratitude was so serious. Seneca lists the crimes that will always be with us, murder, tyranny, theft, adultery, sacrilege and treason, and then says the ungrateful man is worse than all of them, because almost every great crime grows from ingratitude (1.10, paraphrased). The Gospels assume the same instinct. Of ten lepers healed, one came back, a Samaritan, and fell at Jesus's feet, and Jesus asked where the other nine were: "Was no one found except this foreigner to return and give glory to God?" (Luke 17:17 to 18). The return of thanks was the thing a gift was meant to set moving.

The Gospels show benefaction working inside Jewish towns as well. The elders of Capernaum plead for a Roman centurion with the words a city might carve on a stone: "This man is worthy to have You grant this, for he loves our nation and has built our synagogue" (Luke 7:4 to 5). Jesus knew the language and turned it. "The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those in authority over them call themselves benefactors. But you shall not be like them" (Luke 22:25 to 26). Benefactor, euergetes, was a title rulers and cities used with pride. Jesus sets beside it the youngest and the servant.

Faith belonged to the same world. The Greek pistis and the Latin fides meant trust, trustworthiness and faithfulness, the bond that held relationships together, among people and between people and their gods. Teresa Morgan, in Roman Faith and Christian Faith (2015), shows how much of the Roman world ran on it and argues that the first Christians did not invent a new meaning for the word so much as turn it toward God and Christ. Her work doesn't shrink faith to loyalty alone, since belief that something is true belongs to it too. But a first hearer of "faith" would hear a relationship, a person to rely on and to be loyal to, more than an opinion held in private.

John Barclay's Paul and the Gift (2015) gives readers a way to see what was new in Paul's grace without pretending the ancients knew nothing of generous gifts. He names six ways a gift can be thought perfect, or carried to its extreme: its size (superabundance), the giver's pure goodwill (singularity), its coming first, before the receiver has done anything (priority), its being given without regard to the receiver's worth (incongruity), its power to change the receiver (efficacy), and its expecting nothing back (non-circularity). Barclay finds every one of them in ancient talk about gifts except the last: nearly everyone assumed a gift rightly created a return. Paul, on his reading, stresses incongruity. Grace comes to the unworthy, and it still calls for a life given back.

Here Seneca and the Gospels meet and then part. Seneca wrote that if you would imitate the gods, you must give even to the ungrateful, for the sun rises on the wicked too (4.26). Jesus used the same picture: the Father "causes His sun to rise on the evil and the good" (Matthew 5:45) and "is kind to the ungrateful and wicked" (Luke 6:35). Yet Seneca's book begins by complaining that people scatter their gifts at random instead of choosing worthy receivers, and much of it is advice on giving wisely. Jesus tells his hearers to lend expecting nothing in return and to fill their tables with people who cannot repay (Luke 6:35; 14:12 to 14). Paul draws the line plainly: one might dare to die for a good man, "But God proves His love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:7 to 8).

read.text: So Jesus declared, “The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those in authority over them call themselves benefactors. But you shall not be like them. Instead, the greatest among you should be like the youngest, and the one who leads like the one who serves.
read.note: Benefactor was an honored public title, carved on statue bases and given to kings. Jesus doesn't call generous rulers wicked. He says their way of turning gifts into rank isn't the pattern for his followers, and he makes the youngest and the servant the measure of greatness.

read.text: But love your enemies, do good to them, and lend to them, expecting nothing in return. Then your reward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High; for He is kind to the ungrateful and wicked.
read.note: This is the line where the Gospel leaves the ordinary rules of gift and return. Lending was expected to bring repayment, and favor was expected to bring loyalty. Jesus grounds his command in God's own way of giving, to people who will not give back, and promises that those who give this way will be sons of the Most High.

read.text: “Were not all ten cleansed?” Jesus asked. “Where then are the other nine? Was no one found except this foreigner to return and give glory to God?”
read.note: The healed foreigner does what every ancient reader knew a receiver of favor should do, coming back to give honor in public. The nine are not said to have done anything wrong by the law; they went to the priests as told. Jesus's question shows he was looking for the return of thanks as well as obedience.

parts.title: The table, the guest and the body
parts.line: Who you welcomed, where they sat and what touched whom all said, in public, what a person was worth.
body: A welcome had its parts, and everyone knew them. When a Pharisee named Simon invited Jesus to dinner (Luke 7:36), a woman known in the town as a sinner came in and wept over his feet. Jesus answered Simon's silent disapproval by naming what the host had left out: "you did not give Me water for My feet ... You did not greet Me with a kiss ... You did not anoint My head with oil" (7:44 to 46). Water, a kiss and oil were the courtesies that told a guest he was honored. Interpreters differ on whether Simon meant a slight or simply did the minimum. Either way, the uninvited woman gave what the host withheld, and Jesus said so in front of the whole table.

Who you ate with said who you were. The complaints against Jesus are almost all about meals: "This man welcomes sinners and eats with them" (Luke 15:2), and of Zacchaeus, "He has gone to be the guest of a sinful man" (Luke 19:7). To accept a man's bread was to accept his standing and lend him yours. The site's guide on hospitality traces the welcome of strangers from Abraham's tent to the early church; the point here is that every table was also a public statement.

Where you sat was a ranking that everyone could read. Proverbs had long advised, "do not stand in the place of great men; for it is better that he says to you, 'Come up here!' than that you should be demoted in the presence of the prince" (Proverbs 25:6 to 7). Jesus's advice about wedding banquets says the same thing almost word for word (Luke 14:8 to 10) and then turns it into a rule about God: "everyone who exalts himself will be humbled" (14:11). He goes further still and tells the host to invite "the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind" because "they cannot repay you" (14:13 to 14), which cut the circle of invitation and return at its root. James found the old ranking alive in the church, where a man with a gold ring was offered "a seat of honor" and a poor man told to stand (James 2:2 to 3).

Open doors could be abused, and the early churches guarded them. The Didache, a short church manual usually dated to the late first or early second century, says a traveling apostle is to be welcomed as the Lord, but may stay one day, or two if there is need; if he stays three, he is a false prophet. When he leaves he is to take nothing but bread for the road, and if he asks for money he is a false prophet. Ordinary Christian travelers may stay two or three days, and anyone who wants to settle must work (Didache 11 to 12). Generosity and honor both depended on the guest not turning the host into a mark.

The body was the most public thing a person owned. The anthropologist Mary Douglas, in Purity and Danger (1966), described dirt as matter out of place and argued that a society's rules about the body often mirror the boundaries it guards. Scholars of the Context Group used her work to read the Gospels. In Jesus's world, purity marked who could come near God and who could share a table. A Pharisee who invited Jesus "was surprised to see that Jesus did not first wash before the meal" (Luke 11:38), and Peter, entering a Gentile's house, told the household, "You know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with a foreigner or visit him" (Acts 10:28). Jesus moved the line inward: "Nothing that enters a man from the outside can defile him" (Mark 7:15). The site's guide on clean and unclean takes up the laws of Leviticus themselves.

Shame lived on the body too. Honor sat on the head and the face: a guest's head was anointed, and a shamed person's face was covered. "Shame has covered my face," says the psalmist (Psalm 69:7). The Bible's first picture of shame is a body that has to be hidden. Before the fall, "the man and his wife were both naked, and they were not ashamed" (Genesis 2:25); after it, they sew fig leaves, and the man says, "I was afraid because I was naked; so I hid myself" (3:10). Stripping a person in public was the deepest insult that world knew, which is why it appears in the story of David's envoys and at the cross.

read.text: And turning toward the woman, He said to Simon, “Do you see this woman? When I entered your house, you did not give Me water for My feet, but she wet My feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair. You did not greet Me with a kiss, but she has not stopped kissing My feet since I arrived. You did not anoint My head with oil, but she has anointed My feet with perfume.
read.note: Each line sets the host's omission against the woman's excess: no water but tears, no kiss of greeting but kisses on the feet, no oil for the head but perfume for the feet. Jesus speaks to Simon while looking at the woman, and in front of the guests he turns the table's judgment of her upside down.

read.text: “When you are invited to a wedding banquet, do not sit in the place of honor, in case someone more distinguished than you has been invited. Then the host who invited both of you will come and tell you, ‘Give this man your seat.’ And in humiliation, you will have to take the last place. But when you are invited, go and sit in the last place, so that your host will come and tell you, ‘Friend, move up to a better place.’ Then you will be honored in front of everyone at the table with you.
read.note: This is ordinary wisdom about saving face, older than Jesus, and Proverbs had said it. But the passage doesn't stop at etiquette. The next verse makes God the host who seats the humble, and the verses after it tell the host to fill his table with people who can never invite him back.

read.text: Suppose a man comes into your meeting wearing a gold ring and fine clothes, and a poor man in shabby clothes also comes in. If you lavish attention on the man in fine clothes and say, “Here is a seat of honor,” but say to the poor man, “You must stand” or “Sit at my feet,” have you not discriminated among yourselves and become judges with evil thoughts?
read.note: The seat of honor followed the church into its own meetings. James calls the habit of ranking guests by their clothes a matter of becoming "judges with evil thoughts." It shows how quickly the old scale reasserted itself even among people who had been taught that it was overturned.

parts.title: Men, women and the public eye
parts.line: The ideals written by men put women indoors; the evidence shows women owning, trading, giving and being honored in public.
body: This is the part of the honor model most open to misuse, so it needs care. Anthropologists of the 1960s described a pattern in which men's honor was won in public competition while women's honor lay in modesty and sexual reputation, guarded by fathers and husbands. Biblical scholars took the pattern over. Later anthropologists, feminist anthropologists among them, found these generalizations too tidy, and the debate that followed changed the field. Crook argued that the challenges of honor crossed lines of gender as well as rank. What follows separates what ancient men said women should do from what the evidence shows women doing.

The prescriptions are real. Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher of Jesus's generation, wrote that markets, council halls and law courts belong to men, while women are best suited to the management of the house (Special Laws 3.169 to 171, paraphrased). Plutarch, a Greek writer and a younger contemporary of Paul, advised a new bride to worship only the gods her husband believes in and to shut her door to strange rites and foreign superstitions (Advice to the Bride and Groom 19). Ben Sira, writing in Jerusalem early in the second century BC, calls a daughter "a secret anxiety to her father" and tells him to keep strict watch over her, or she may make him a laughingstock to his enemies (Sirach 42:9 to 11, in the New Revised Standard Version). For a woman with no children, the shame was public too. When Elizabeth conceived, she said the Lord had "taken away my disgrace among the people" (Luke 1:25).

But ideals are not descriptions, and these are ideals written by men. The evidence of what women did is wider. On a stone found near Corinth, five decrees honor Junia Theodora, a woman with a Roman name living in Corinth, for the help she gave to Lycians who came to the city. The federal assembly of Lycia and the cities of Myra, Patara and Telmessos thanked her in public, and R. A. Kearsley places her around the middle of the first century (Tyndale Bulletin, 1999). Her honor was earned, inscribed and seen. The capable wife of Proverbs 31 "appraises a field and buys it" and trades linen with merchants, and the poem ends, "let her works praise her at the gates" (Proverbs 31:16, 24, 31), the public place where the elders sat. Lydia and Phoebe, women of means and patrons of the first churches, appear in the Roman world portrait.

The churches met in houses, and that blurred the line further. Carolyn Osiek and Margaret MacDonald, in A Woman's Place (2006), describe the house church as a crossroads between public and private. A meeting in a home was a household gathering and a public assembly at once, and women who headed households were hosting the church in rooms that were, by the old map, their own.

The Gospels show both the expectation and the break with it. When the disciples came back to the well in Samaria they "were surprised that He was speaking with a woman" (John 4:27), and none of them dared ask why. Then the woman went into her town, and "many of the Samaritans from that town believed in Jesus because of the woman's testimony" (4:39). On Easter morning the apostles "did not believe the women" (Luke 24:11), and the women were right. The Gospels don't pretend the old expectations were absent. They record them, and then they let the women be the ones who were believed by God first.

Two warnings close this part. First, the evidence is uneven: most ancient texts were written by men of means, and the lives of poor women, slave women and village women are mostly glimpsed through what others said. Second, nothing here describes any living culture or community. Words like honor and shame are sometimes used today as if they explained whole peoples; they do not, and the critics of the model were right to say so.

read.text: Just then His disciples returned and were surprised that He was speaking with a woman. But no one asked Him, “What do You want from her?” or “Why are You talking with her?”
read.note: The disciples' surprise tells the reader what was expected: a teacher did not hold a long public conversation with a woman he did not know, least of all a Samaritan. Their silence tells the reader they knew better than to challenge him. Twelve verses later the town believes because of her word.

read.text: “The Lord has done this for me. In these days He has shown me favor and taken away my disgrace among the people.”
read.note: Childlessness was a private grief and a public verdict at once. Elizabeth speaks of her disgrace "among the people," the shame of a woman whose neighbors had drawn their conclusions. God's gift answers both, the grief and the standing.

read.text: Give her the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her at the gates.
read.note: The gates were where the elders sat and judged and where a man's name was made, and the same poem says her husband "is known at the city gate" (31:23). The poem asks that her own works be praised there. Even Israel's wisdom tradition did not keep a woman's honor indoors.

parts.title: Shame and vindication in Israel's Scriptures
parts.line: Long before the Gospels, Israel prayed about shame, and its stories turn on a good name lost and given back.
body: The language of honor and shame did not reach the Bible from the Greeks. It runs through the Hebrew Scriptures from the start. When the new king of Ammon suspected David's envoys of spying, he "shaved off half of each man's beard, cut off their garments at the hips, and sent them away" (2 Samuel 10:4). The men were "thoroughly humiliated," and David told them to wait in Jericho until their beards grew back before they came home (10:5). The insult was aimed at David through his messengers, and the Ammonites knew it: when they "realized that they had become a stench to David," they hired an army (10:6). A beard and a robe started a war.

The psalms are full of the prayers of people whose name is at stake. "Do not let me be put to shame; do not let my enemies exult over me" (Psalm 25:2). "Let me never be put to shame; save me by Your righteousness" (Psalm 31:1). "I am a worm and not a man, scorned by men and despised by the people. All who see me mock me" (Psalm 22:6 to 7). The shame these prayers fear is not chiefly an inner feeling. It is public defeat: the enemy's gloating, the sneer of the onlookers, the verdict of the crowd that God has abandoned this person. What they ask for is vindication, God acting where all can see, so that the one who trusted him is shown to have been right. "You, O LORD, are a shield around me, my glory, and the One who lifts my head" (Psalm 3:3).

The same book holds the other register too. Psalm 51 is the great prayer of guilt: "Against You, You only, have I sinned and done what is evil in Your sight" (Psalm 51:4). Israel prayed about both, a conscience before God and a name before people, sometimes in the same breath, without choosing between them. That's the best answer to the idea that some cultures feel only shame and others only guilt.

Isaiah's servant speaks of shame borne on purpose: "I offered My back to those who struck Me, and My cheeks to those who tore out My beard. I did not hide My face from scorn and spittle" (Isaiah 50:6). The same servant is sure of the outcome: "I know that I will not be put to shame" (50:7). The Gospels tell the night of Jesus's trial in words that echo it: "some of them began to spit on Him" and struck him in the face (Mark 14:65).

Ruth is a story about a family's name. Naomi comes home bereaved and says, "I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty" (Ruth 1:21). Her daughter-in-law is a Moabite, from a people the law kept out of the assembly (Deuteronomy 23:3), gleaning in other men's fields. Boaz praises her loyalty and blesses her in the name of the God "under whose wings you have taken refuge" (Ruth 2:12). When she asks him, "Spread the corner of your garment over me" (3:9), she uses the same Hebrew word, kanaph, wing or corner: he is to be the shelter he prayed for. The nearer kinsman refuses because he would "jeopardize my own inheritance" (4:6). Boaz pays the cost "to raise up the name of the deceased," so that it "will not disappear ... from the gate of his home" (4:10), and the women of the town end the story praying, "May his name become famous in Israel" (4:14). A widow's honor and a dead man's name are restored by a man who spends his own.

Jesus's parable of the father and two sons runs on the same values. The younger son asks for his share of the estate while his father is alive (Luke 15:12), a hard break with the honor a son owed. When he comes back, "while he was still in the distance, his father saw him and was filled with compassion. He ran to his son, embraced him, and kissed him" (15:20). Kenneth Bailey, in Poet and Peasant (1976), drew on the village life he knew in the modern Middle East to argue that a dignified older man in long robes did not run in public, so the father takes the shame of the road on himself. That is a modern parallel, not ancient evidence. But the ancient ideal of dignity points the same way: Aristotle says the great-souled man has a slow step, a deep voice and an even way of speaking, because hurry belongs to someone who takes too many things seriously (Nicomachean Ethics 4.3, 1125a). The father then calls for "the best robe," a ring and sandals (15:22), giving the son back his standing before the household before anyone else can rule on it. And he leaves his own feast to plead with the older son outside (15:28).

read.text: in You, my God, I trust. Do not let me be put to shame; do not let my enemies exult over me. Surely none who wait for You will be put to shame; but those who are faithless without cause will be disgraced.
read.note: Shame here is the triumph of enemies and the collapse of a trust that everyone can see. The prayer is that God will not let the one who waits for him be publicly proved a fool. In the next breath the psalmist asks for something else as well: "Remember not the sins of my youth" (25:7). Shame and guilt sit together in one prayer.

read.text: So Hanun took David’s servants, shaved off half of each man’s beard, cut off their garments at the hips, and sent them away. When this was reported to David, he sent messengers to meet the men, since they had been thoroughly humiliated. The king told them, “Stay in Jericho until your beards have grown back, and then return.”
read.note: Half a beard and a garment cut at the hips: the insult was precise, public and aimed at the body. David's response protects his men first, keeping them out of sight until they can return with their honor restored. The story shows how seriously the Old Testament world took a shamed body.

read.text: So he got up and went to his father. But while he was still in the distance, his father saw him and was filled with compassion. He ran to his son, embraced him, and kissed him.
read.note: Every verb is fast: saw, ran, embraced, kissed. Whatever one makes of the modern village parallels, the father reaches the son before the son can finish his speech or the town can make up its mind. The welcome comes first, and it comes in public.

parts.title: The cross and the overturned scale
parts.line: Rome built the cross to say a man was nothing, and the first Christians made it the center of their boast.
body: Every part of this portrait meets at the cross. Crucifixion was the most shameful death that world knew, and it was designed to be. The site's guide on crucifixion and shame sets out Martin Hengel's evidence: a punishment for slaves, bandits and rebels, carried out naked and in public. Cicero, prosecuting a governor who had crucified a Roman citizen in 70 BC, called it "the cruelest and most disgusting penalty" (Against Verres 2.5.165, crudelissimum taeterrimumque supplicium), and in another speech said the very word cross should be kept far from a citizen's body, thoughts, eyes and ears (For Rabirius 16). For Jews, Deuteronomy had said that "anyone who is hung on a tree is under God's curse" (Deuteronomy 21:23), and Paul quotes it of Christ (Galatians 3:13).

To claim a crucified man as Lord was to claim honor for the person the whole system had judged worthless. Outsiders said so. Justin Martyr, writing in Rome about AD 150, reports that critics called it madness for Christians to give a crucified man the second place after the unchanging and eternal God (First Apology 13). Paul knew the reaction in advance: "we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles" (1 Corinthians 1:23).

Rather than soften the shame, the New Testament writers used it. Hebrews says Jesus "endured the cross, scorning its shame, and sat down at the right hand of the throne of God" (Hebrews 12:2). He neither escaped the shame nor accepted its verdict. He treated the judgment of the crowd as weightless and was given the highest seat in the only court that finally counts. The same letter places the cross "outside the city gate," the place of the excluded, and asks its readers to "go to Him outside the camp, bearing the disgrace He bore" (13:12 to 13). They had already been "publicly exposed to ridicule" and lost property for their faith (10:33 to 34). Instead of telling them the shame is unreal, the letter tells them whose company they're in.

Philippi was a Roman colony proud of its rank, and Joseph Hellerman, in Reconstructing Honor in Roman Philippi (2005), read the hymn of Philippians 2 against the Roman course of offices, the cursus honorum, by which an ambitious man climbed from post to post. Paul tells Christ's story as a descent instead, which Hellerman calls a course of shame, cursus pudorum: equal with God, then a servant, then a man, then obedient to death, "even death on a cross" (Philippians 2:6 to 8). Then the judgment is reversed from above: "God exalted Him to the highest place and gave Him the name above all names" (2:9). Paul sets this before a church and says, "Let this mind be in you" (2:5).

Paul turned the same scale over in Corinth. "Not many of you were wise by human standards; not many were powerful; not many were of noble birth" (1 Corinthians 1:26). God "chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise" and "the lowly and despised things of the world, and the things that are not, to nullify the things that are" (1:27 to 28). Of himself and the other apostles he wrote, "You are honored, but we are dishonored" (4:10). The first Christians didn't stop caring about honor. They changed courts. The apostles left the council "rejoicing that they had been counted worthy of suffering disgrace for the Name" (Acts 5:41). Peter told believers who suffered for the name Christian, "do not be ashamed, but glorify God that you bear that name" (1 Peter 4:16). Paul wrote, "I am not ashamed of the gospel" (Romans 1:16).

The old contest stayed, but it was turned around. "Outdo yourselves in honoring one another," Paul tells the Romans (Romans 12:10): the race for honor is still run, but now the prize is to give it away. And the shame didn't vanish either. It was carried. In a world where worth was granted by the crowd and could be stripped in an afternoon, the gospel told of a God who took the most shameful place there was and made it the place of his glory. A thoughtful reader can decline to believe that and still see what it would mean if it were true: no verdict of any crowd would be final again.

read.text: Let us fix our eyes on Jesus, the author and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy set before Him endured the cross, scorning its shame, and sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.
read.note: The word translated scorning means to think little of, to treat as of no account. Jesus didn't dodge the shame of the cross; he refused to let it be the true verdict. The verse ends with the highest place of honor in the ancient world, a seat at the king's right hand.

read.text: But God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise; God chose the weak things of the world to shame the strong. He chose the lowly and despised things of the world, and the things that are not, to nullify the things that are,
read.note: Paul uses the honor scale's own words, wise and strong, lowly and despised, and turns them over. God shames the honored by choosing the shamed. For a church where status still mattered at the table, this was no abstract theology; it was a new way to rank everyone in the room.

read.text: And so Jesus also suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood. Therefore let us go to Him outside the camp, bearing the disgrace He bore.
read.note: Outside the gate was where the crucified died and where the unclean were sent. The letter doesn't ask its readers to bring Jesus inside to respectability. It asks them to go out to him and carry the same disgrace, in the confidence that the city they seek is still to come (13:14).

ancient.name: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics
ancient.note: 4.3 (1123b: honor the greatest of the external goods; 1125a: the slow step and level speech of the great-souled man). Fourth century BC.

ancient.name: Ben Sira (Sirach, Ecclesiasticus)
ancient.note: 42:9 to 11, on a father's watch over a daughter. Written in Jerusalem early in the second century BC; quoted here in the New Revised Standard Version.

ancient.name: Cicero, Against Verres and For Rabirius
ancient.note: Against Verres 2.5.165 (crucifixion as the cruelest and most disgusting penalty, 70 BC); For Rabirius 16 (the word cross kept far from a citizen).

ancient.name: Philo of Alexandria, On the Special Laws
ancient.note: 3.169 to 171: public places for men, the house for women. A Jewish philosopher of Jesus's generation. Paraphrased.

ancient.name: Seneca, On Benefits
ancient.note: 1.1 (gifts scattered at random); 1.3 (the Three Graces); 1.4.2 (benefits bind human society); 1.10 (the ungrateful man worse than other criminals); 4.26 (give even to the ungrateful, as the sun rises on the wicked). Written by Paul's contemporary, who died in AD 65. Paraphrased.

ancient.name: Josephus, Life
ancient.note: 1 to 6: his priestly and Hasmonean pedigree, which he says he took from the public records. Written in the 90s AD.

ancient.name: Plutarch, Table Talk and Advice to the Bride and Groom
ancient.note: Table Talk 5.7 (a dinner conversation about the evil eye and envy); Advice to the Bride and Groom 19 (a wife to worship her husband's gods). Late first and early second century AD.

ancient.name: The Didache
ancient.note: 11 to 12: how churches received traveling apostles, prophets and ordinary Christian travelers. Usually dated to the late first or early second century.

ancient.name: Justin Martyr, First Apology
ancient.note: 13: critics call it madness to give a crucified man the second place after God. Rome, about AD 150.

ancient.name: Lucian, The Passing of Peregrinus
ancient.note: 13: Christians taught that they are all brothers and worship "that crucified sophist" (A. M. Harmon's translation). Written soon after AD 165.

ancient.name: Origen, Against Celsus
ancient.note: 3.55: Celsus, a critic of the later second century, on Christian workers who turn children from their fathers. Origen replied about the middle of the third century.

ancient.name: Tertullian, Apology
ancient.note: 39: pagans resent that Christians call one another brothers. North Africa, about AD 197. Paraphrased.

ancient.name: Inscriptions and mosaics
ancient.note: The decrees for Junia Theodora on a stele found near Corinth (first century AD); the evil eye mosaic from the House of the Evil Eye at Antioch (second century AD), now in the Hatay Archaeology Museum.
